title: Judge rightly (John 7:1–24)
hook: at the harvest festival of booths, he teaches in secret then openly

segments.voice: Yesterday, many walked away, and Peter asked: Lord, to whom shall we go? Your line was to whom else?

Each autumn, Jewish families who keep Sukkot build a little hut: walls of wood or cloth, a roof of branches loose enough to see the stars through. For a week they eat in it, and some sleep in it. It's called a sukkah, a booth, and the festival is Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles. Jews still keep it today. Today's chapter of John opens as that feast approaches, and Jesus's own brothers are pushing him: go up to Jerusalem, show yourself to the world.
screen: `A HUT WITH A ROOF OF BRANCHES.`

segments.voice: "Now the Jews' feast of tabernacles was at hand." Tabernacle is an old word for a tent. The law of Moses told Israel to live in booths for seven days, remembering the wilderness years, when God's people lived in tents and God kept them. It was a harvest festival too, full of joy. John is honest about family: "For neither did his brethren believe in him." Jesus says his time hasn't come and stays behind. Then, after they leave, he goes up anyway, quietly, not openly. In Jerusalem, people are whispering: he's a good man; no, he's leading people astray. Halfway through the feast, he walks into the temple courts and teaches out loud. People are amazed: "How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?" He hasn't studied under any teacher they know. He's from Galilee. They're judging by appearances, and he knows it. Then he takes up the sabbath healing again. You circumcise a baby boy on the sabbath, he says, when the eighth day falls on it, so the law of Moses isn't broken. Why be angry with me for making a whole man well on the sabbath? It's a careful argument from inside Jewish practice. And he ends: "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment." A man from Galilee with no teacher might be a teacher. A healing on the sabbath might be keeping the sabbath, not breaking it.
screen: then, large: `JUDGE NOT ACCORDING TO THE APPEARANCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've judged quickly, by their clothes, their accent, their job, or one thing they said. Then imagine what you don't know, what they carry, what they've survived, what they might be good at, and let your picture of them get a little bigger. If you pray, ask to see them as God sees them; if you don't, hold them with more curiosity than you did a minute ago.
Sukkot. The Jewish feast of booths, kept each autumn, that this day's chapter opens as Jerusalem prepares for it.
Your line: judge not by appearance. The surface is only the start of a person. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians read this chapter as part of John's story of Jesus at the great Jewish feasts; Jews today keep Sukkot each autumn by building and eating in a sukkah.

chat.meaning: The crowd judged him by where he came from. He said: judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

notes: Index word is 'Feast of Tabernacles'; index title 'Judge rightly'. Both kept.
Circumcision on the eighth day overriding the sabbath was accepted practice (cf. Mishnah Shabbat 18:3–19:2). The 'lesser to greater' (qal vahomer) argument style: confirm the trapdoor.
Jesus described as 'a craftsman from Galilee' (tekton, Mark 6:3; John itself doesn't name his trade). Changed in review from 'builder', since carpenter/builder/craftsman is debated. Confirm.
Hook (from index) says 'he teaches in secret then openly'; John 7:10 says he went up in secret, then taught openly (7:14). Voice and fork are accurate; consider rewording the index hook.

'His brothers': churches understand Jesus's brothers differently (Catholic: cousins or relatives; Orthodox: Joseph's children from an earlier marriage; many Protestants: younger sons of Mary). The script doesn't explain this; consider whether a note is needed.
